options.text: Shard orders by customer id across several Postgres primaries behind an application routing layer

decision: Where should the 900 GB of customer-generated JSON documents live?
context: There are 3 million documents averaging 300 KB, read whole 95 percent of the time and patched in small pieces otherwise, with 3 times as many expected within two years. The team knows Postgres and has no document database, and the existing Postgres cluster runs at 70 percent CPU at peak.

options.name: objects
options.text: Whole documents as compressed objects in object storage with an index row in Postgres

options.name: jsonb
options.text: JSONB columns in the existing Postgres cluster, with patches applied in SQL

options.name: docdb
options.text: A managed document database storing each document as one record with partial updates

options.name: dedicated
options.text: A separate Postgres cluster for documents, with JSONB columns and its own scaling

decision: How should the platform deliver outbound webhooks to 2,000 customer endpoints?
context: The platform sends 5 million events a day, some customer endpoints take up to 30 seconds to respond, and enterprise customers ask for guaranteed delivery with 7 days of replay. Six engineers own the platform, and a hosted delivery service would cost 4,000 dollars a month at this volume. Payloads contain customer email addresses, which the security team prefers to keep inside the company's own cloud account.

options.name: pull
options.text: A cursor-based events API that customers poll, in place of pushing to their endpoints

options.name: queue
options.text: A queue-backed worker pool with per-endpoint retries, backoff, and a circuit breaker

options.name: pubsub
options.text: A managed pub/sub service with push subscriptions pointing at each customer endpoint

options.name: hosted
options.text: A third-party hosted delivery service that receives each event and sends it to customers

decision: How should the team bring its metrics backend's 25 million active series under control?
context: A customer id label multiplies the series count, and the self-hosted metrics store is at 85 percent of memory with queries timing out during incidents. Support and product rely on per-customer latency views, and the observability team has two engineers.

options.name: hostedvendor
options.text: Move to a hosted metrics vendor that bills per active series and manages scaling

options.name: recording
options.text: Add recording rules that aggregate away pod labels and expire raw series after two days

options.name: droplabel
options.text: Remove the customer id label and answer per-customer questions from logs and traces

options.name: scaleout
options.text: Add memory and shard the store by service team behind a global query layer

decision: How should the team handle its flaky browser tests?
context: A 40-engineer monorepo has 6,000 tests, and about 3% of CI runs fail from flakes at 14 minutes per rerun. Around 20 browser end-to-end tests cause most flakes, and they cover checkout and sign-in flows that were behind two incidents last quarter. Feature work is committed through the end of the quarter.

options.name: quarantine
options.text: Move known flaky tests into a non-blocking suite and track each one with an owner

options.name: autoretry
options.text: Retry each failed test automatically twice and block merges when all attempts fail

options.name: freeze
options.text: Pause feature merges for one sprint while the whole team fixes the flaky tests

options.name: replace
options.text: Replace the flaky browser tests with contract and component tests against a stubbed backend

decision: How should compatibility between services be verified before release?
context: Eight teams own REST services that call each other and release independently up to five times a day, and five of the last nine incidents were integration mismatches. Most of those involved changed meaning, such as units or status semantics, rather than changed shapes, and no team has written a contract test before. The shared 38-minute end-to-end suite catches about half of them but fails weekly from staging drift.

options.name: contracts
options.text: Consumer-driven contract tests in every service pipeline, verified against each provider's published contracts

options.name: sharedsuite
options.text: Keep the shared end-to-end suite as the release gate and invest in stabilizing staging

options.name: canary
options.text: Replace pre-release integration suites with canary rollouts that roll back automatically on elevated error rates

options.name: smoke
options.text: Run ten cross-service smoke journeys after every deploy and halt promotion when one fails

decision: What release cadence should the web and mobile product follow?
context: A 12-person team ships a web app that deploys in 10 minutes plus native mobile apps with store review times of one to three days. Support wants predictable release notes, product wants experiments live within days, and two enterprise customers require advance notice of visible UI changes.

options.name: weeklytrain
options.text: Ship every client on a fixed weekly release train with a Thursday code freeze

options.name: continuous
options.text: Deploy web continuously from main and release each mobile build as soon as features complete

options.name: darklaunch
options.text: Merge all work dark behind feature flags and enable features per customer through scheduled rollouts

options.name: monthly
options.text: Cut a monthly release branch with a stabilization week where only fixes are accepted

decision: How should code review work on this team?
context: Nine engineers see a median first-review wait of 26 hours on pull requests averaging 600 lines, and two seniors perform about 70% of reviews. Only those two know the billing module, where defects reach customer invoices. Many large pull requests are generated migrations and framework upgrades that cannot be split.

options.name: smallprs
options.text: Require small stacked pull requests and rotate reviewers across the team with a response-time target

options.name: owners
options.text: Route reviews through code owners so each module's owners approve and everyone else can comment

options.name: pairing
options.text: Pair on risky changes and merge them directly, with lightweight asynchronous review for everything else

options.name: selfmerge
options.text: Let tenured engineers merge after CI passes, with weekly audits of sampled merged changes

decision: How should the frontend codebase be structured for five squads?
context: Twenty-five engineers in five squads work in one React app with a 14-minute build and weekly merge conflicts in shared routing, and two squads want independent deploy schedules. A redesign of the shared navigation lands within six months, and the last cross-team migration stalled at 60%.

options.name: modular
options.text: Keep one app and enforce module boundaries with lint rules and per-squad code ownership

options.name: microfe
options.text: Split into micro-frontends deployed independently and composed at runtime by a shared shell application

options.name: packages
options.text: Move to a workspace monorepo of separately built packages that ship as one deployed app

options.name: routeapps
options.text: Split into separate apps per top-level route group, served behind one domain with path routing

decision: How should the app load and cache server data on its screens?
context: A React app with 140 CRUD screens uses three different fetching styles and has 30 open bugs about stale data. Two screens need realtime updates, the team of six is evaluating server rendering for SEO within the year, and a previous library migration stalled midway.

options.name: querylib
options.text: Adopt a query-caching library and migrate screens incrementally whenever the team touches them

options.name: store
options.text: Centralize all server data in a global normalized store with one shared update path

options.name: serverload
options.text: Move data loading into route loaders and server components as part of a framework migration

options.name: ownhook
options.text: Standardize on one small in-house fetch hook with explicit invalidation helpers for every screen

decision: How should mobile and web clients fetch data from the backend services?
context: Web and native mobile clients call services owned by three backend teams, and mobile screens make six to nine REST calls per view on slow networks. Backend teams ship independently on different schedules and have full roadmaps through next quarter, and the mobile screens are due for a rebuild in about four months.

options.name: graphql
options.text: Expose a GraphQL gateway over the services with a schema co-owned by the backend teams

options.name: bff
options.text: Build a thin backend-for-frontend per client that aggregates service calls for each screen

options.name: restexpand
options.text: Keep plain REST and add field selection and embedded-resource parameters to existing service endpoints

options.name: batch
options.text: Keep existing endpoints and add one batch endpoint that executes several REST calls per request

decision: How should partners receive event notifications from the platform?
context: Forty partner integrators consume about 5 million events a day, ranging from hobbyists to enterprises behind strict firewalls, and about a quarter need events within five seconds. Thirty percent of support tickets concern missed events, and two engineers maintain all partner integrations.

options.name: webhooks
options.text: Push signed webhooks with automatic retries and a dashboard where partners can replay failed deliveries

options.name: polling
options.text: Offer a cursor-based events endpoint that partners poll at the pace their systems allow

options.name: streaming
options.text: Provide a long-lived streaming connection with resume tokens so partners continue from their last processed event

options.name: queue
options.text: Publish events to a managed queue per partner, read with credentials scoped to that partner

decision: How should the team keep third-party dependencies patched?
context: Fifteen services in four languages pull in about 1,200 transitive dependencies, and the scanner reports roughly 90 advisories a week, most of them low severity. Reachability analysis works for only two of the languages, two engineers can spend four hours a week on patching, and a customer contract sets a seven-day window for criticals. Automated test coverage is above 80% on most services.

options.name: updatebot
options.text: Enable an update bot that opens grouped weekly pull requests and auto-merges green ones

options.name: triage
options.text: Triage each advisory by reachability and patch only the ones judged exploitable or critical

options.name: cigate
options.text: Fail CI builds on any high-severity advisory, with a documented exemption path for each exception

options.name: quarterly
options.text: Pin and vendor dependencies, upgrade in quarterly batches, and patch criticals out of band immediately

decision: How should engineers get access to production data when debugging?
context: Thirty engineers regularly inspect production records to diagnose customer bugs, about a third of which depend on exact production values, and on-call engineers currently hold standing read access. A compliance audit is due in three months, and a support admin tool already exists but covers few record types.

options.name: jit
options.text: Grant time-boxed access on request, approved by a second engineer, with every query logged

options.name: standing
options.text: Keep read-only standing access for the on-call rotation, with query logging and quarterly access reviews

options.name: replica
options.text: Provide a sanitized nightly replica and remove all direct engineer access to production data

options.name: admintools
options.text: Build curated admin-tool views for support cases that expose specific records without raw database access

decision: How should the team plan and schedule its work?
context: A ten-person product team runs two-week sprints, but about a third of each sprint goes to unplanned interrupts and velocity varies by 40% between sprints. Stakeholders ask for quarterly delivery dates, two neighboring teams sync on a shared two-week rhythm, and the team's biggest projects each take about five weeks.

options.name: sprints
options.text: Keep two-week sprints and reserve a fixed buffer of capacity for interrupt work

options.name: kanban
options.text: Move to continuous flow with WIP limits and forecast dates from cycle-time percentiles

options.name: cycles
options.text: Adopt six-week cycles with fixed time and variable scope, followed by a two-week cooldown

options.name: rotation
options.text: Keep sprints but rotate one engineer weekly as dedicated interrupt handler outside the sprint scope

decision: How should the team fund its technical debt work?
context: Twelve engineers have committed roadmap work for the next two quarters, and deploy frequency fell from daily to weekly over the past year because of a brittle build pipeline. Leadership wants features, and engineers report debt scattered across 20 modules.

options.name: tax
options.text: Reserve 20% of every sprint for debt items that the engineers choose themselves

options.name: burst
options.text: Run one debt-only sprint each quarter with agreed measurable targets reviewed by leadership

options.name: scout
options.text: Fund debt only when it blocks planned features, and clean modules as features touch them

options.name: pipeline
options.text: Assign a rotating pair to the build pipeline full time for two months

decision: How should UI regressions in the shared design system be caught?
context: A design system of 70 components is consumed by six apps and must support three browsers. UI regressions reach production about twice a month, designers review changes in design files rather than code, and the screenshot service bills per image.

options.name: visual
options.text: Run screenshot comparisons on every component story in CI, reviewed by a designer on changes

options.name: behavior
options.text: Write behavior-focused component tests that assert roles and text, run in a real browser

options.name: appflows
options.text: Add a few browser end-to-end tests for critical flows inside each consuming application

options.name: staged
options.text: Release each design-system version to one consuming app first and promote it after a week

decision: How should the team limit the damage from bad deploys?
context: A service deploys 15 times a day at about 200 requests per minute, and four bad deploys last quarter took 22 minutes on average to recover. Two of them could not be rolled back because of a schema migration, and a third corrupted data quietly without tripping any metric check.

options.name: rollback
options.text: Automate one-click rollback to the previous build and rehearse it in a scheduled monthly drill

options.name: rollforward
options.text: Treat deploys as roll-forward only and ship small fixes behind flags within the hour

options.name: progressive
options.text: Deploy to five percent of traffic first and halt expansion when automated metric checks regress

options.name: soak
options.text: Add a manual approval gate and a thirty-minute staging soak before every production release
